candidates.raw_excerpt: In Orbit Aerospace has swapped reentry vehicles for autonomy software, and NASA and the Space Force are funding the shift.  The Torrance, CA-based startup has won new government contracts for its onboard AI system, which the company says can run a spacecraft’s operations without waiting on ground control. “We’re scaling to the point where you simply can’t have one, or even more, ground operators monitoring the satellite,” In Orbit CTO and cofounder Ishaan Patel told Payload. “When the problem scales that far, I think we need to have an increased sense of autonomy for the vehicle.” Ground control: In Orbit was founded in 2020 as an in-space logistics company building reentry vehicles. However, with a handful of companies already working building the return route from space, the team felt that the market just wasn’t ready for another player.  “We were just slightly too late,” In Orbit CEO and cofounder Ryan Elliott told Payload.  The team pivoted to tackling a different reentry problem. Plasma around a returning vehicle can cut off GPS and comms, so if something goes wrong mid-descent—such as one side of the vehicle overheating—no one on the ground can see it or react in time.  In Orbit’s proposed fix is onboard autonomy software and ground interface for operators—dubbed INTELLACT. The software-only system is designed to manage spacecraft health, execute maneuvers, and respond to anomalies onboard, using a vehicle’s existing hardware. On the ground, INTELLACT feeds operators context, and recommends next steps instead of raw telemetry. INTELLACT is slated to debut in Q1 2027 on the AFRL/NASA HyperSTEP mission, running in shadow mode. Patel said the aim is to move humans from “in the loop” to “on the loop,” where “the ground operator is the architect of the mission.” The company is also building StratoDrop—an autonomous paraglider that deploys from high-altitude balloons to deliver cargo. candidates.raw_excerpt: Reflect Orbital, the startup attempting to offer sunlight on-demand with in-space mirrors, announced the purchase of two launches today from Indian launcher Skyroot Aerospace. The deal includes: One launch on Skyroot’s Vikram-1 launch vehicle, which debuted in July , and can carry ~350kg to LEO. One launch on Skyroot’s upgraded Vikram-1U vehicle, which is expected to fly its first mission in Q1 2027, and will be capable of carrying ~550kg to LEO. Reflect Orbital did not disclose the cost of each launch, or when the missions would fly. Precious inventory: The deal comes amid a launch capacity crisis that has forced some operators to buy their own dedicated vehicles, as SpaceX has stopped accepting reservations after 2029 for its popular Transporter rideshare program. Despite that, companies are still finding ways to get to orbit. For example, in August, Portal Space Systems announced it purchased a full SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket for Portal’s Motus Via Sol mission in 2028. Portal doesn’t expect to fill the Falcon 9 to the brim, however, and made a deal with Maverick Space Systems who later filled most of the available space with 10 Kepler satellites. A spokesperson from Reflect Orbital told Payload the company “is the primary and only payload at this time.” Blinding lights: In July, Reflect Orbital received FCC approval to fly its first in-space mirror-satellite—Eärendil-1—but the company’s larger plan is to fly a constellation of ~50,000 mirrors to provide sunlight on Earth after dark. The idea is to use the constellation to provide extra sunlight for terrestrial solar farms to generate power after sunset, but the company also plans to provide sunlight for everything from search-and-rescue operations, to nighttime concerts. candidates.title: Scientists discover that some of the universe's biggest explosions may have never happened at all
candidates.raw_excerpt: Now you see them, now you don't. Scientists have discovered that some of the universe's most powerful explosions, hypernovas, may not happen at all. These explosions, known as hypernovas , were first proposed to explain unusual stars in the halo of our galaxy, the Milky Way , and in a neighboring dwarf galaxy. It was suggested that these stars could only form from the debris of an explosion 10 times more powerful than the 'average' supernovas . The team behind these new findings suggests that ordinary supernovas could actually account for these stars when the uneven or non-spherical way they fling out matter is considered. "If we look at a supernova today, the star's materials are not spread evenly. Oxygen might predominantly fly in one direction, sulphur in another. New stars might form from a mix of pieces of the supernova, not its overall mix of elements," team leader Anmol Aggarwal of University College London (UCL) said in a statement. "We developed mathematical models that took account of this and found in all cases that stars with a very unusual mix of ingredients were most likely formed from ordinary supernovas. "All the evidence we see for hypernovae is suddenly gone." Hypernova vs. supernova: What's the difference? Supernovas occur when massive stars run out of fuel for nuclear fusion , effectively ending their lives. This results in the star's core collapsing, sending shockwaves rippling through its outer layers, causing explosions we call supernovas. Hypernovas are proposed to occur in a similar way, but for an even more massive and rapidly spinning star. This results in a vastly more energetic explosion. When supernovas or hypernovas happen, they fling elements that the dying star has forged throughout its lifetime into their surrounding cosmic environments. These elements eventually become the building blocks of the next generation of stars. That means analyzing the chemical signatures of stars can tell stellar scientists about their family histories.

An OpenAI engineer has been arrested after allegedly installing a hidden audio recording device inside the company's office in San Francisco, the United States, according to statements released by the US Department of Justice (DOJ) and OpenAI.

OpenAI said in a post on X that it had "discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices" and "referred the matter to the FBI."

There is currently no evidence that the individual improperly accessed or exfiltrated model weights, source code or customer data, the company added.

OpenAI's security team discovered the device on September 30 during a routine inspection. The employee, a Saudi national, was arrested on October 9, the DOJ said.

According to the DOJ, Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer who had worked for OpenAI since July 2025, allegedly wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and inserted it into a television in an executive conference room.

Closed-circuit television footage from the company's office showed that Alfozan "appeared near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device's discovery," although he was not authorized to attend meetings held there.

He also used a "productivity tool" to search for information about OpenAI's office buildings, meeting rooms, calendars, schedules and people's locations, according to the DOJ statement.

Before joining OpenAI, Alfozan had reportedly worked at other major technology companies, including Meta and Microsoft.

The FBI investigation is ongoing.

Small artificial intelligence (AI) models may be only months away from being able to behave like computer worms, copying themselves from one internet-connected device to another without human intervention, AI giant Anthropic said.

The finding could open a new front in the cybersecurity threats emerging from AI, which have rattled governments and companies rushing to adopt the technology.

The research, published on an Anthropic blog late Monday, comes as tech companies race to build increasingly powerful AI capabilities directly into phones, laptops, cars and household devices, rather than running them only in distant data centers.

A computer worm is malicious software that spreads between machines on its own. Researchers at Anthropic said an AI version would no longer need powerful data centers to operate.

Instead, it could hop from device to device across networks of cheap, poorly secured consumer hardware, such as smart TV boxes and kitchen appliances.

The researchers based their calculations of how far such a worm could spread on Kimwolf, a botnet, or network of hijacked devices controlled by hackers, that infected more than two million devices at its peak, mostly off-brand Android TV boxes.

candidates.title: Federal Reserve Says AI Data Center Buildout Is Making Everything More Expensive
candidates.raw_excerpt: It’s not just your electricity bill that could be going up — it sounds like the massive boom in AI data centers is making practically everything more expensive. As the Washington Post reports , officials at the Federal Reserve are starting to sing a different tune after blaming president Donald Trump’s tariff war on rising prices, admitting that the explosion in “AI-related investments” is contributing to inflationary pressures. That’s on top of Trump’s Iran war already sending the price of oil soaring. Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago president Austan Goolsbee told Semafor that AI-tied inflation is “jumping out of its lane.” “Prices are going up in spaces that are not just components in data centers and the directly adjacent industries,” he said. “I’m getting increasingly nervous that that’s just straight, old-fashioned overheating demand.” In economics, overheating occurs when aggregate demand outpaces productive capacity, leading to demand-side inflation, higher prices, and eventually reduced demand and consumption. In the worst case scenario, overheating can even trigger a recession . “It takes a long time for overheated demand to get going, and once it’s going, it’s hard to get rid of that,” Goolsbee added. While the prices for groceries have yet to be directly impacted, economists are wondering whether it’s only a matter of time. Charles Messier was scanning the sky for objects that could confuse comet hunters when he catalogued the galaxy as M51. However, Messier wasn't able to see the spiral structure, and he didn't identify it as a galaxy. Eventually, Edwin Hubble found out that M51 and other features like it were actually galaxies. The smaller galaxy to the right is NGC 5195, which is actually more distant than M51, and not next door. (Image credit: NASA/ESA/S. candidates.title: Earth's poles shifted surprisingly fast during the age of dinosaurs, ancient sea levels reveal
candidates.raw_excerpt: The location of Earth's geographic poles has changed several times over the past 320 million years in a process known as true polar wander, according to measurements of ancient flooding brought about by sea level changes resulting from our planet's crust shifting relative to Earth's spin axis. Such a shift can affect climate, both on local scales and globally, as regions that were by the poles find themselves moving down to lower latitudes and vice versa. This can then affect atmospheric circulation patterns, which affect climate across the world. The changes would have affected the environments in which life developed and evolved, from the age of the dinosaurs through to some of our oldest primate ancestors. True polar wander is not the same as a change in the rotational axis of the Earth . Currently, Earth spins at an angle of 23.4 degrees relative to the plane of its orbit around the sun, and this rotational axis can vary periodically over tens of thousands of years as a result of the Milankovitch cycles caused by the gravitational pull of the sun and planets. True polar wander is different. Here, the angle of Earth's spin axis does not change relative to its orbital plane. Instead, Earth's crust and mantle shift relative to that rotational axis. This is because Earth is not perfectly spherical. Instead, it is oblate, with Earth's rotation causing the equator to bulge out and the poles to slightly flatten. Because Earth is not spherical, it has multiple axes of inertia, the largest one being aligned with the rotational axis. These axes need to be balanced to prevent Earth's rotation from becoming chaotic. However, plate tectonics and indeed the Milankovitch cycles can upset that balance of mass, for example by causing more continental crust to congregate in one hemisphere than another. candidates.title: China releases report on ethical governance for embodied AI
candidates.raw_excerpt:
China on Tuesday released a report on the ethics of embodied intelligence – the field that covers machines that can sense, decide and act in the physical world.

The report treats embodied intelligence ethics as part of broader AI ethics. It flags six risk areas: harm to human autonomy, to social relationships and to development rights; physical injury and threats to public safety; privacy violations and misuse of personal information; bias, discrimination and exclusion from services; identity misidentification and overestimation of capabilities; and unclear accountability, with incidents hard to reconstruct.

The report defines five risk levels, R1 through R5, based on how serious the consequences are. It also sets out six basic governance principles: human-centered, safe and controllable, privacy-protecting, fair and inclusive, transparent and explainable, and accountable and traceable.

Ethical requirements should be built into every stage of an embodied AI product's lifecycle – design, R&D, deployment, operation and service, and decommissioning – and each stage should have clear protection requirements and assigned responsibilities, said Zhang Shizong, deputy director of the IT Research Center at the China Electronics Standardization Institute (CESI).

Zhang said the safeguards work in three ways. Limits on what the machine can do to protect physical safety. Controls on what it can collect to protect sensory data. Clear signals that it's a machine, plus ways to switch it off, preserve the user's ability to choose.

China will accelerate work on national standards including guidelines for ethical governance for AI and embodied intelligence, Zhang said.

candidates.title: Astronaut captures mesmerizing auroras with iPhone from ISS | Space photo of the day for Oct. 13, 2026
candidates.raw_excerpt: Earth's night side is wreathed in colorful auroras in a new smartphone image captured from the ISS. (Image credit: Anil Menon, NASA) NASA astronaut Anil Menon captured a gorgeous view of the northern lights dancing over the night side of Earth from the International Space Station on Oct. 10 using an iPhone camera. What is it? Menon's photo reveals spectacular pink, purple and red auroras glowing in Earth's upper atmosphere above a sparse dappling of city lights, subtly blurred by the motion of the orbital spacecraft over the course of the exposure. Bright stars glimmer between the solar panels and outer hulls of the ISS and visiting spacecraft, painted purple by the auroral display. "Flying through is rare and amazing," Menon wrote in a separate aurora video he posted to X on Oct. 10. "You can see the lights on the outside of [the] station reflecting back like Christmas LEDs. It's definitely more immersive." Why is it amazing? Menon captured the auroras during a period of heightened geomagnetic activity, after several coronal mass ejections (CMEs) struck Earth's magnetic field, triggering geomagnetic storms ranging from minor (G1) to strong (G3) over the weekend. During geomagnetic storms, more charged particles are accelerated along Earth's magnetic field lines toward the polar regions, where they collide with gases in the upper atmosphere; they excite them, causing them to release energy as light and producing spectacular auroral displays. The blue-purple colors seen in Menon's image are largely produced by nitrogen at altitudes of around 60-120 miles (100-200 kilometers) , while the red hue comes from oxygen atoms higher up, typically above 125 miles (200 kilometers). The photo is particularly impressive because it was captured on an iPhone camera, as opposed to the more traditional Nikon cameras that astronauts sometimes use to capture Earth during their time aboard the ISS. candidates.title: Khushi Shah, Orbiventure
candidates.raw_excerpt: Growing up, Khushi Shah thought working in space meant a career path in the engineering industry.  However, Shah was eventually drawn to more “creative parts” of the industry and is now creating art that’s touched down on the lunar surface.  First steps: Shah joined the Space Generation Advisory Council in India—and got a taste of leadership as their Asia-Pacific communications manager. “That opened a lot of doors for me…making people understand why space is really important in at least 10 different countries.” That rapidly brought Shah lunarside. Shah spoke to the founder of Space Pride, who in turn referred Shah to the Interstellar Foundation, which was building the ASPIRE One Record—a time capsule of human history and culture inspired by the Voyager Golden Record—for a Moon landing.  Touch down; Working with fellow artist Rania Djojosugito, the resulting art portrayed a colorful black hole surrounded by rainbows. The piece—which is part of the 1GB of content on the project—actually made it to the Moon twice, aboard Firefly Aerospace’s Blue Ghost Mission 1 and Intuitive Machines’ IM-2. “I kind of built my whole life living up to that dream, or trying to achieve that impossible goal,” Shah said, recalling wanting to touch the Moon as a child.  What’s next: More recently, Shah moved to New York City and successfully completed a design program at the Parsons School of Design, while also working there as a research assistant. Shah is also working with Orbiventure, as a contract service designer looking at how environmental and satellite data is used for fisheries.  “The work spans community research, co-design facilitation, and adoption testing, starting with fisheries and expanding into agriculture and environmental justice. candidates.title: Kayla Bigham, FAA
candidates.raw_excerpt: Kayla Bigham grew up wanting to be an astronaut. Then, after learning about the Apollo 1 and Apollo 13 emergencies in elementary school, her goal shifted—she knew she wanted to keep space exploration safe. Bigham, 27, is now living out that dream as a flight-safety analyst at the FAA’s Office of Commercial Space Transportation. In her job, she analyzes rockets and reentry capsules looking to fly, and studies—in a worst-case scenario—how to ensure the public remains safe from space debris. “There are definitely industries—nuclear is a great example—where huge disasters have stunted an industry that otherwise could bring a lot of good,” she told Payload. “I would hate to see that happen to space.” Go boom: Bigham’s first job was investigating fire and gas explosions in the oil and gas industry, to provide evidence after a disaster. While this first job was outside the space industry, she credits the role with preparing her for the FAA. She points to a lot of overlap: the two positions are very safety-oriented, and study how failures can cause property damage and personal harm. New horizons: Working for the FAA, Bigham says every day offers a new challenge. “If I was doing design work for a company, I’d be looking at the same system on the same rocket for months,” she said. “I’m looking at every system on every rocket to get a holistic picture.”  She’s also gotten to be on the front lines of developing Part 450, the new regulations that aim to ease burdens for launchers seeking permission to fly, though these regulations have faced some criticism from industry. Bigham has a message to those who claim the government is seeking to stifle commercial space innovation. “Our entire office is very pro-commercial space. I think sometimes regulators get a bad rep for being difficult, or you don’t want to see [the industry] succeed, but we champion every success,” she said. “We want the industry to succeed. candidates.title: Brianna Clark, Vast
candidates.raw_excerpt: Los Angeles residents had a special space sight in 2012 when Space Shuttle Endeavour arrived atop a 747, before being ferried through city streets for a permanent exhibit at the California Science Center.  Brianna Clark remembers her elementary-school teachers telling students to look up as the spaceship flew by. Last November, all of us could have looked up again to see Clark’s own contributions to a spaceship aboard the Vast Haven demo, which tested out tech that will one day support humans living in LEO Building the future: Clark, a propulsion engineer at Vast, said she is excited to also work on Haven-1’s launch NET Q1 2027. “It provides so much opportunity for not just people who love aerospace, but everyday people,” she explained. “We’re doing science for medical research. We’re doing science for pharmaceuticals, everything that patches and impacts everyday life.” Clark always had aspirations to be an aerospace engineer. Her childhood projects, like “satellites” made of coffee cans and aluminum wrapping, led to student work at California State University, Long Beach building experimental small rockets.  Clark took on internships at several name-brand companies, including Relativity Space, Blue Origin, and Vast. She also was accepted into the Zed Factor Fellowship class of 2024, and was a Brooke Owens Fellow for the class of 2026.  The big payoff: One of Clark’s favorite parts of aerospace engineering is seeing “stuff that you worked on touch space. That is such a surreal feeling,” she said. And she says her experience is not so unique, as space applications are quickly opening up access for all of us. “Everyday people can also look up to [space] and see it as their access, and their accessibility,” she said. “In previous space programs, it’s this huge division of how normal people get into space. And I think with commercial, we’re trying to bridge that gap now.” The post Brianna Clark, Vast appeared first on Payload .

candidates.title: Tyler Bernstein, Zeno Power
candidates.raw_excerpt: Growing up, Tyler Bernstein’s favorite NASA missions—from Mars rovers to Voyager’s interstellar journey—all had one thing in common: They all ran on nuclear batteries.  Now, Bernstein is CEO of Zeno Power, where he works on nuclear-battery technology to power NASA’s return to the lunar surface—and anywhere else humans want to explore, where solar panels won’t work and diesel can’t reach.  Origin story: Bernstein caught “the bug for building” in a high-school computer-science class, and went to Vanderbilt University expecting to end up at Google or Amazon. Then, in his sophomore year, he and a friend wrote a paper on flying a Boeing 777 on nuclear power. “We had zero business looking into putting a nuclear reactor in a Boeing Triple Seven, but that changed the direction of our lives,” he said. In 2018, Bernstein and his cofounders launched Zeno Power. With support from the university and NSF, the idea shifted from airliners to drones, then to something bigger—the deep sea, the Arctic, and space were becoming contested, and none of them had reliable power. The Zeno team immediately began talking to as many people as they could, from four-star generals to members of Congress.  “This was really curiosity and grit that brought us into a lot of conversations, and over time, the passion has grown,” Bernstein said. He eventually took leave from Vanderbilt to run the company full time, also earning a spot in the competitive Thiel Fellowship.  Tech deep dive: Nuclear batteries aren’t new. But each unit has been built one at a time, fueled with one of the world’s rarest materials. Zeno wants to build hundreds a year, using more abundant fuel.  “That model worked when demand was one spacecraft going to Pluto,” Bernstein said. “It doesn’t work now that NASA has announced a permanent Moon Base.” In June, Zeno established its nuclear battery manufacturing facility at the Vallecitos Nuclear Center in Sunol, CA. candidates.title: Amanda Nguyen, AIA
candidates.raw_excerpt: It took just 66 years to get from the Wright brothers’ first powered flight to landing humans on the Moon—a fact Amanda Nguyen loved pointing out as a student educator at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum. Today, Nguyen is working to make sure space policy can still keep up. Nguyen’s dad, an engineer at both Orbital and Northrop Grumman, “brainwashed” her into thinking space was cool, she told Payload. As she “just wasn’t STEM-minded,” the museum showed her that not everyone in space is an engineer. “As a political-science major, I knew I wasn’t going to design rockets or build satellites,” she said. “But I understood I could contribute by shaping the policies that enable those missions.” Cleared for takeoff: As senior manager of space systems at the Aerospace Industries Association (AIA), Nguyen runs the group’s space-regulatory portfolio. Launching a rocket or accessing spectrum “runs through a policy, a procedure, a bureaucracy,” she said. She turns members’ feedback on what is and isn’t working into unified industry responses to rule-makings. “We’re not bending metal,” she said. “I just want to keep the path that they’re on as clear as possible.” That often means pushing regulators to reflect “where technology and markets are heading, not just where they are today.” Ground game: Much of Nguyen’s attention now goes to what happens before liftoff. candidates.title: Anna Shaposhnik, ORBES
candidates.raw_excerpt: Each astronaut hour in orbit costs $130,000. What if robots could help with some of the grunt work—while also giving the world a better view of living in space? That’s the founding thesis behind ORBES, an in-space robotic startup founded in 2024 by Anna Shaposhnik.  Origin story: The 24-year old met NASA Astronaut Terry Virts when she was a student at the University of Southern California, doing a degree in arts, technology, and the business of innovation. Virts, who shot footage for the IMAX documentary A Beautiful Planet while aboard the ISS, talked about the challenges of both filming and working in orbit.  Hence, ORBES was born. Shaposhnik, who serves as its CEO, believed she could build robots to provide practical and artistic support for space missions.. Ticket to ride: The CA-based company has two products. ORB—designed for missions inside space stations—is set to head to the ISS for the first time next year, in partnership with Voyager Technologies. EXO-ORB—which will capture exterior footage of space structures—will fly on the demo mission of Symphony Space’s Adagio platform in late 2027 or early 2028. The big (motion) picture: The tech has immediate practical applications, such as allowing companies to inspect the exterior of sats and spacecraft. But Shaposhnik sees those missions as laying the ground for longer-term partnerships with STEAM applications, including filming movies in-orbit or collecting footage that can allow everyone to experience space stations through virtual reality. “It’s like a go-to market strategy. Right now there’s a lot of infrastructure operators thinking about, ‘How do I get infrastructure built and working?’ The ability to capture external footage for both engineering review and communication purposes is actually the most urgent need right now,” she said. “We get our foot in the door through being able to capture external views, but we’re also going to be trusted as the operators to be able to maintain their structure.

candidates.title: Bryce Kelly, Deloitte
candidates.raw_excerpt: In DC, even the happy hours are out of this world.  At Space Happy Hour, people all over the industry attend—which is why Bryce Kelly, a strategy and transformation consultant at Deloitte, loves making regular appearances to connect friends with opportunities. Growing up in Seattle, WA, Kelly says he naturally fell into following off-Earth activities in that “big aerospace town.” That lifelong interest turned into a career while he was majoring in international relations at Pomona College in southern California, after an aspiring-space-lawyer classmate showed him that the space industry included more than just engineers.  “I started researching,” Kelly said. “I was like, ‘Oh my, gosh, wait. The space industry is a thing that I can go into, even as a non-technical person.’” From there, he quickly secured space-related internships in DC at the National Defense Industrial Association, as well as the US Commerce and State departments. Helping hand: Kelly landed at Deloitte in 2024, not too long after wrapping up his degree with a thesis on the Artemis Accords, showing the US-led initiative has extensive international consultations. Today, his job involves highlighting the work the consultancy does in space—for example, Deloitte has nine active satellites, according to Kelly—as well as helping clients understand the opportunities and realities of working in the commercial space sector. Projects have ranged from lunar communications to space-industry forecasts, with Kelly’s role moving between project management and providing advice, as the situation requires. And when Kelly is not at work, he continues to network—including as project manager for the UN-affiliated Space Generation Advisory Council, a global non-profit for students and young professionals. “Some people have more experience working in the space sector, but I think I’m just very gung-ho,” Kelly said of his approach at work, and outside. candidates.title: Ashling Sugarman, Pepperdine Law School
candidates.raw_excerpt: Not many people can turn a childhood dream of being a “space cowgirl” into a career, but Ashling Sugarman is getting close. She’s just traded a lasso for law books. After studying international business as an undergrad at Pepperdine University, Sugarman spent three years at an intellectual property firm, where it finally clicked. “I realized, oh my goodness, you could take science and law and put it together, and this is so cool,” she told Payload. Saddle up: Sugarman returned to Pepperdine for law school already set on space. Her first-year summer at the Space Court Foundation (SCF) convinced her she didn’t have to follow the big-law track—she could chart her own path. That path ran straight to the FCC Space Bureau, where she was the Front Office’s first intern during the bureau’s Part 100 licensing overhaul. “I was constantly in awe every single day,” Sugarman said. “They would find just such creative ways to handle a certain issue.” Rules of the range: Sugarman brings that same creativity to her research. In SCF’s Student Space Law Journal, she drew on aviation and maritime traffic rules to argue that the seven factors in the EU’s proposed Space Act—for deciding which satellite operator must move—don’t make sense in their current order, and suggested a new one. At the 2026 International Space Development Conference, she presented a quantified framework that lets operators calculate how important a right-of-way maneuver is to them. “You can kind of say, ‘OK, this is my value. What’s yours?’ Whoever is the lower one, you have to maneuver,” she said. New frontiers: At this year’s International Astronautical Congress in Antalya, Turkey, Sugarman presented on who should govern a lunar-time standard—and how to get rivals like the US and China to agree on one. Back home, she’s finishing her final year at Pepperdine while working remotely as a legal extern with Blue Origin’s FL-based legal enterprise team. She hasn’t fully hung up the lasso, though—she still rides horses

candidates.title: Hayley Blyth, Bird & Bird
candidates.raw_excerpt: Hayley Blyth’s path into space started with a question about war: how do the rules of armed conflict apply in orbit? She embraced the question as a law student in Canberra, Australia, writing her thesis on the intersection of international humanitarian law and space operations. The research put her in touch with the Australian Space Agency—and pulled her toward a field where the rulebook was still being written. Both sides of the table: After about two years at a telecom law firm, Blyth joined the Australian Space Agency as in-house legal counsel, helping build the country’s regulatory framework for launches and ground stations.  Four years ago, she moved to London for a taste of a bigger space industry. After a stint at a three-person boutique firm, Blyth joined international law firm Bird & Bird, where she co-heads the global Space and Satellite practice—a role she stepped into as an associate. Square pegs: These days, Blyth’s favorite problems are the ones the law never saw coming. Many existing regulatory frameworks were “designed at a time when that kind of technology didn’t exist,” Blyth said, leaving in-orbit servicers and orbital data centers squeezed into boxes built for something else. Give each new technology its own rulebook, and you get a patchwork of regimes that “don’t fit together,” she said. “And then what happens when the technology goes even further, and suddenly we’ve got all these things in one?” But one broad regime has to stretch to cover everything. “It’s a bit of a puzzle,” she said. Phone home: One of the puzzles playing out in real time is D2D. Satellite phones aren’t new, Blyth noted, but a mass commercial rollout is. As regulators were facing some of these questions for the first time, Blyth advised companies launching the first satellite D2D services in the UK and EU.  To help others keep up, she built Bird & Bird’s publicly available Satellite D2D Regulatory Tracker. candidates.title: Pasha Kravtsov, True Anomaly
candidates.raw_excerpt: As a kid, Pasha Kravtsov was an avid gamer, and got upset when other kids cheated. “I always wanted to understand: How were they doing that?” he told Payload. As an adult, he’s still asking that question—but now his sights are set a bit higher. As True Anomaly’s cybersecurity director, Kravtsov leads a team of 27+ people working out how to stop someone from breaking into a spacecraft. Side quests: Kravtsov spent his teen years reverse-engineering games, finished high school early, and joined Cloudflare’s support team at age 17. His parents even had to sign the offer letter. Within a year he’d moved to security, where he worked on a bug that leaked private data from sites using Cloudflare. He left after the company’s 2019 IPO and bounced between startups. Then, Russia invaded Ukraine, where Kravtsov’s family is from. “Commercial satellites became battlefield infrastructure overnight,” he said. When a former colleague shared that his company was working to counter a recently-launched Russian military sat, Kravtsov wanted in. Cheat code: He joined True Anomaly in early 2023 as its first security engineer—with no aerospace or defense background—and built the encryption for the company’s first mission. “A lot of the problems I was working on, you can’t just Google,” he said. Commercial software can feel like “an abstraction layer on an abstraction layer,” he said. But in defense space, “it’s very, very clear what the stakes are.” “A bad day at Cloudflare didn’t mean a physical effect,” Kravtsov said. In orbit, a hijacked satellite could go “somewhere where it’s not supposed to be,” with real consequences for national security missions.  Multiplayer mode: The team got its biggest test earlier this year. True Anomaly was one of the first companies to face NOAA’s new, stricter cybersecurity requirements for spacecraft licenses—arriving shortly before the company’s Mission X-3 launch. Kravtsov worked out a plan with the agency and led the effort to meet the requirements

candidates.title: Mickey Matthew, WarpWare
candidates.raw_excerpt: “I grew up assuming going to space was easy,” Mickey Matthew told Payload. His family moved to Houston, TX, when he was nine, and in middle school a friend canceled weekend plans because a parent was going to space. With seven friends who had astronaut parents, going to space felt like something everyone was doing.  As he later found out, it wasn’t—and part of the reason is that nearly every spacecraft team rebuilds its software from scratch. As cofounder and COO of WarpWare, Matthew is hoping to give teams a head start with flight-ready software instead.  “”A five-person team with a good idea shouldn’t need three years and a nine-figure budget to get a vehicle talking to the ground,” he said. Making the leap: Matthew studied aerospace engineering at Texas A&M University, interning at NASA Goddard before landing a job at Sierra Space when it had ~300 employees. As Sierra grew its workforce to 3,000, Matthew went from hands-on testing with astronauts to business development to deputy chief engineer, even presenting to investors. While at Sierra, Matthew asked his friend Alex Reynolds —who led flight software integration at Sierra—how much existing code could be reused for a new vehicle. “The answer to that turned out to be zero,” he said. The payload companies they talked to were stuck in the same loop. “It’s like having to reinvent Microsoft Word before you can write a document,” Matthew said. So, in 2023, he and Reynolds co-founded WarpWare, whose tools cover digital twin testing, flight software and mission operations. candidates.title: Priya Abiram, Vast
candidates.raw_excerpt: Priya Abiram once thought she was the stupidest student in her technology class. Today, she’s an astronaut life-support-systems engineer at Vast preparing for a spaceflight NET next year aboard Virgin Galactic. Abiram’s mission will study menstruation in microgravity for Operation Period, a non-profit founded by crewmate Manju Bangalore. “I will be the youngest research astronaut, which is very exciting,” Abiram, 22, told Payload.  Rocket dreams: Her journey to space began in KSC’s Rocket Garden, where she admired the “huge machines that touch the sky” at just seven years old. After that, Abiram vowed to study rockets. None of her family members were in aerospace, requiring Abiram to learn in unfamiliar environments —including that technology class in eighth grade. “I was very quiet, didn’t talk to anyone,” Abiram recalled. But at year’s end, her teacher held a model-rocketry competition. Abiram poured her heart into it and was shocked when she won. “It was like, ‘Wow, I can actually do this, and maybe I could go to space.’” Onwards and upwards: Since school was short on practical experiences to prepare for spaceflight, her mother suggested joining the Air Force’s Civil Air Patrol (CAP), a volunteer civilian auxiliary to the Air Force. CAP helped Abiram gain confidence and connections, including a mentor who is now in the Space Force.  Inspired by her mentor’s confidence working a room, Abiram started her own CAP aerospace program, teaching 150 students STEM skills like rocketry and robotics. The program quickly scaled nationally, gaining Abiram her first internship at Boeing while still in high school.  Next, Abiram attended Cornell University, completing her undergrad and masters within four years, while racking up internships at places like KSC, Blue Origin, and Vast. candidates.title: Ellie Chalphin, In-Q-Tel
candidates.raw_excerpt: Ellie Chalphin’s career has mostly been about trying to make things move, whether its rocket parts across borders or launch contracts through NASA. Now at In-Q-Tel, Chalphin is tackling one of the most challenging moves yet—moving startup technology into the hands of the government. As manager of space partnerships at the CIA-chartered venture firm, Chalphin is working at the intersection of founders, investors, and the defense and intelligence agencies that might buy what they build. Things that go boom: As an undergraduate researcher with MIT’s Election Data + Science Lab, Chalphin studied how local voting rules shaped turnout and got hooked on “outdated regulations…that aren’t aligned with how quickly the technology is moving.” That led her to Raytheon, supporting missile programs in Tucson, AZ, and naval systems in Rhode Island. “I love things that go boom,” Chalphin told Payload. “I didn’t go to space camp, and I didn’t take AP physics,” she said. “But now that I’m here, I’m like, oh, these are definitely my people.” Eat your veggies: In 2021, she joined SpaceX’s international trade team, working with four federal agencies on export controls, launch licensing, and hazmat permits. It is a tame comet because it can be anticipated. It is wild because it is still fresh and bright; the brightest of all the recurring comets. It is the only one that periodically becomes conspicuous to the naked eye. Halley through history Before 1986, Halley had been seen and recorded on 29 occasions. In A.D. 66, observers described it as a sword in the skies above Jerusalem. In 1066, its image was woven into the strip of linen now known as the Bayeux Tapestry , where an agitated crowd of Saxons points toward a fiery comet we know to be Halley. In 1301, the Florentine painter Giotto di Bondone witnessed the comet and was so impressed that, a few years later, he depicted a comet as the star that led the Magi to Bethlehem in one of his magnificent frescoes in Padua's Scrovegni Chapel . More recently, Halley passed unusually close to Earth in 1910. As the 1986 return approached, people who remembered that earlier appearance likely told their children and grandchildren about being awakened before dawn and taken outside to see a huge, ghostly, gleaming object in the sky. Halley's earlier appearances suggested that each return to the inner solar system might produce a magnificent display. Little wonder, then, that the public expected great things in 1986. candidates.title: A faint glow from the early universe could help solve the mystery of dark energy
candidates.raw_excerpt: Hydrogen may be the most common element in the cosmos, but scientists could use it to do something unique: uncover the nature of dark energy, the mysterious force driving the accelerating expansion of the universe. This new line of dark energy investigation comes from the fact that researchers have determined that the CHIME (Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) project can detect the faint radio glow of hydrogen from the universe's distant past. Not only does this represent a faster and much less expensive way to investigate dark energy, but it is a major milestone for CHIME. The instrument was specifically devised to investigate dark energy and its pervasive influence. "This is a completely new technique for probing the cosmos, delivered by an instrument that was conceived and built by Canadians," CHIME principal investigator Mark Halpern of the University of British Columbia said in a statement . "It's a bold new step in the global cosmology program and a Canadian success story." Why is dark energy so problematic? Dark energy is the mysterious force that is accelerating the expansion of the universe . It is so problematic for scientists because it started acting on the fabric of space only after the expansion triggered by the Big Bang had halted. That's akin to pushing a child on a swing, watching it stop, and then seeing the swing start up again without a push. And, not only that, but the swing starts oscillating faster and faster. Consider scientists akin to very worried parents, who would really like to know where this ghostly push came from and how it is going to proceed. Just as, if the push on the swing continues, the child could end up in the bushes, or in orbit, the strengthening of dark energy could result in the cold death of the cosmos, or even a " Big Rip " scenario that sees space shredded. Alternatively, if it weakens and allows gravity to reassert dominance, then the universe could collapse back in on itself, resulting in a " Big Crunch "

candidates.raw_excerpt: SpaceX just broke an uncharacteristically long Starlink launch drought. The company sent 27 of its Starlink internet satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO) today (Oct. 12), launching them atop a Falcon 9 rocket from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base at 8:28 p.m. EDT (5:28 p.m. local time; 0028 GMT on Oct. 13) It was the first Starlink mission for a Falcon 9 since Sept. 19 , which was another 27-satellite liftoff from Vandenberg. For some perspective on this recent gap: Between Aug. 19 and Sept. 6, a span of 19 days, SpaceX launched seven Starlink missions with Falcon 9s. The Falcon 9's first stage rests on the deck of a ship at sea shortly after the Oct. 12 launch. (Image credit: SpaceX) SpaceX did loft a batch of Starlinks after that, but it wasn't aboard a Falcon 9. The company's Starship megarocket carried 26 next-gen Starlink V3 craft on its 14th test flight, which took place on Sept. 28. Starship reached orbit for the first time ever on Flight 14 , and it deployed the Starlinks successfully as well. This will happen many more times going forward, if all goes to plan: The Starlink V3 constellation will eventually consist of about 100,000 satellites , all of which will fly on Starship, Elon Musk has said. Indeed, SpaceX plans to sunset the Falcon 9 and its cousin, the Falcon Heavy , in the next few years, shifting their duties over to the fully reusable, far more powerful Starship, which remains in the test-flight phase. That shift will be a big one for the spaceflight community, for the Falcon 9 is the workhorse rocket of its generation. SpaceX and NASA are preparing to fly a resupply cargo flight to the International Space Station on Tuesday morning. The pre-sunrise launch will be SpaceX’s 35th mission to the orbiting outpost as part of NASA’s Commercial Resupply Services (CRS) contract. Liftoff of SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station is scheduled for 6:33 a.m. EDT (1033 UTC). The rocket will fly on a northeasterly trajectory upon leaving the pad. If all goes well, the Cargo Dragon spacecraft, tail number C211, will dock with the zenith port of the Harmony module on Oct. 15 around 11 a.m. EDT (1500 UTC). The space-facing docking port was recently vacated by the Crew Dragon Freedom , which safely delivered the four members of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 mission back to Earth with a splashdown on Oct. 8. Spaceflight Now will have live coverage beginning about an hour prior to liftoff. SpaceX will launch the mission using the Falcon 9 first stage booster B1096. This will be its eighth launch after previously flying NASA’s IMAP, CRS-34, NROL-77, NROL-95, GPS-III 9, Kuiper Falcon 01, and Starlink 6-87. It is the fourth flight for Dragon C211. It’s previous cargo runs included CRS-26, -29, and -33. The spacecraft will remain docked to the ISS for about a month following docking. candidates.raw_excerpt: ispace-Europe and Aerospace Logistics Technology Engineering Company (ALTEC) are set to collaborate on lunar rover testing, mission simulations, and operations training in a new pan-European partnership. ispace-Europe and ALTEC will assess opportunities for ispace-Europe to use ALTEC facilities to simulate rover platform operations in lunar analog environments. The two companies announced the MoU, Oct. 12. ALTEC is a public-private company owned by Thales Alenia Space and the Italian Space Agency (ASI). It operates the Rover Operations Control Center (ROCC), the mission control facility for ESA’s ExoMars Rosalind Franklin rover, which is currently used for ground testing of rover systems. ALTEC is also developing a new Lunar Simulation Center, funded by the Italian Space Agency (ASI), dedicated to the simulation and testing of robotic lunar exploration missions and related operational activities. ispace-Europe is the European subsidiary of Japanese lunar lander company. The agreement will also explore broader cooperation potentially related to lunar exploration technologies, lunar mobility, and space resource utilization. The new facility will aim to provide analog environments and capabilities to support the testing and validation of technologies, systems and operational concepts for future lunar missions, further strengthening Italy’s role in planetary exploration. “Testing, simulation and operator training in analog lunar environments are essential to successful lunar surface operations. Through this collaboration with ALTEC, we have the opportunity to bring together ispace-Europe’s expertise in lunar rover development and operations with ALTEC’s advanced lunar analog facilities, as well as their expertise testing for planetary mission operations. This agreement reflects the growing strength of Europe’s lunar exploration ecosystem,” Julien-Alexandre Lamamy, CEO of ispace-Europe, said in a statement. The black hole sits at the center of the galaxy NGC 1275, located around 225 light-years away, and is the brightest galaxy of the Perseus Cluster . The supermassive black hole first flared in X-rays, which indicated an increase in the rate at which it was accreting matter. Actively feeding supermassive black holes sit in regions called active galactic nuclei (AGNs), with their immense gravity heating surrounding matter, causing them to glow brightly. These emissions are boosted by material channeled to the poles of the central black hole, from where it is blasted out as powerful twin jets that shine across the electromagnetic spectrum , particularly in radio waves. The observation of the following radio jet from the AGN at the heart of NGC 1275 via flaring in radio waves is crucial for understanding the relationship between the disk of matter that surrounds and feeds the black hole, called an accretion disk, and the jets it launches. This so-called disk-jet coupling is key to developing a better picture of how black holes influence star formation in the galaxies in which they sit, and thus the growth of those galaxies. candidates.raw_excerpt: They don't produce anything like the torrent of "shooting stars" associated with August's Perseids or December's Geminids, but the Taurid meteor showers have something else going for them — fireballs. The Taurids are famous for occasionally producing exceptionally bright, slow-moving meteors that can streak dramatically across the night sky from September to December. As a bonus, they're visible from both the Northern and Southern hemispheres. That's because they appear to emanate from the constellation Taurus, which sits close to the ecliptic, the apparent path the sun takes across the sky as Earth orbits around it. The Taurids are actually two closely related showers — the Southern Taurids and Northern Taurids — whose activity overlaps in late October and November. That's why they're known informally by skywatchers as the "Halloween fireballs." The broad overlapping peaks make the Taurids less about watching on one particular night and more about keeping an eye on the night sky for several weeks. Both have their radiant points — the place in the night sky where their "shooting stars" appear to come from — close to the famous Pleiades (M45) open cluster of stars in the constellation Taurus . There's another tempting reason to watch the Taurids in 2026 — moonlight will cause little interference around the main peaks. When are the Southern Taurids? The Southern Taurids are already underway. According to the American Meteor Society , they're active from Sept. 20 through Nov. 20, with two distinct components. The annual component peaks around Oct. 14, while a component particularly associated with fireballs peaks overnight on Nov. 4-5. That's the night to circle if you're hoping to see one of the "Halloween Fireballs." However, don't expect a conventional meteor storm . candidates.raw_excerpt: On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight . This was the first time that a spacecraft carried more than one person into orbit, with three cosmonauts packed inside the spacecraft. Only two cosmonauts were originally supposed to fly on this mission, but Soviet politicians pressured the Russian space program to add one more. This left no room for spacesuits on board, so this also became the first spaceflight without spacesuits . Two of the crewmembers, an engineer and a doctor, became the first civilians to go to space. On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched the first multiperson mission, Voskhod 1, which launched three Russian cosmonauts into space. The crew included Vladimir Komarov (commander), Konstantin Feoktistov (engineer) and Boris Yegorov (doctor), shown at right. (Image credit: Roscosmos) Why it mattered Voskhod 1 served as yet another first for the Soviet Union during a space race kicked off by the launch of Sputnik 1 in 1957 and followed up by the first human spaceflight with Yuri Gagarin in 1961. And while the United States did follow up with its one human spaceflights, until Oct. 12, 1964, every mission had one person on board. That changed with Voskhod 1, which crammed three man into a spacecraft not much larger than the Soviet Union's one-person Vostok spacecraft. At the time, NASA was develoing the two-person Gemini spacecraft , which prompted the Soviet Union's then leader to push for an edge. Scientists believe it’s an example of a skylight — the collapsed roof of an underground lava tube , which forms a circular aperture in the ground. candidates.raw_excerpt: The Etosha Pan, Namibia's largest salt pan, seen from space. (Image credit: Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2026), processed by ESA) A neon blue pool swirls amongst what look like clouds, all surrounded by a bright red stretch of land. This might look like the surface of an alien planet , but it's actually a salt flat right here on Earth , seen from space. What is it? Etosha National Park in northern Namibia hosts the largest salt pan, or piece of land covered with salt and other minerals, in the country. This image of the Etosha Pan was captured on April 5 of this year by Europe's Copernicus Sentinel-2 mission, which consists of two identical satellites in the same orbit. The Sentinel-2 pair observe and capture imagery of our planet in different wavelengths using a high-resolution multispectral imager that can see 13 different spectral bands, or ranges of wavelengths. By looking at our planet from space, and observing it through different wavelengths and colors, we can better understand Earth's topography and how it changes over time. With this image, researchers can better understand this landmark in Namibia, a nation in southwestern Africa. Why is it incredible? While this image is strikingly beautiful, the Etosha Pan doesn't exactly look like this in real life. If you were standing close to the pan in the national park, it would look bright white. While this is a real image, false color has been added, which allows scientists to separate different types of vegetation and topography. With the false color, the vegetation surrounding the salt pan appears in shades of red, while the salt pan itself looks like a mix of bright, light and dark blues with cloudy sediment floating around. candidates.title: Jurassic fossil reveals early mammaliaform adaptations
candidates.raw_excerpt:
An international research team led by Shenyang Normal University has discovered and named Megacauda sungei, the largest known Jurassic docodont mammaliaform. The fossil was found in Jurassic rock formations dating back about 160 million years in Ningcheng County, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. The study was published online in Nature on October 7.

The fossil, housed at the Liaoning Paleontological Museum of Shenyang Normal University, measures about 52 centimeters in length and weighs an estimated 1 to 2 kilograms. It preserves a well-defined skull, a robust torso and a long tail.

The discovery sheds light on the diversity and evolution of Jurassic mammaliaforms, an extinct group that includes modern mammals and their extinct relatives. The specimen's well-preserved throat anatomy and hyoid bones resemble those of modern mammals. These features suggest that the anatomical structures involved in swallowing and suckling had evolved in early mammaliaforms long before modern mammals emerged, according to Li Yikun, associate professor at Shenyang Normal University's School of Paleontology and the study's first author.

The fossil also preserves much of the pelvis, hind limbs and tail vertebrae. Together with its distinctive teeth, these features suggest that Megacauda sungei was adapted to a semiaquatic lifestyle. Its prominent upper canine teeth and shearing cheek teeth indicate that it preyed on small animals, potentially including aquatic prey.

candidates.title: UAE unveils lander for bold 7-asteroid mission set to launch in 2028 (photos)
candidates.raw_excerpt: The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has moved a step closer to launching its second-ever interplanetary mission — an ambitious, eight-year exploration of seven asteroids between Mars and Jupiter that will culminate with a landing on the mysteriously red asteroid 269 Justitia. The mission team unveiled a half-scale model of the homegrown probe that will make that landing during an Oct. 1 press conference in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the UAE. The autonomous craft will ride attached to the main spacecraft MBR Explorer , named after Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid al-Maktoum, the ruler of Dubai and the UAE's prime minister. The flight-ready lander is being kept pristine in a vacuum chamber in the capital before being transported to Colorado by Etihad Airways, officials said, where it will be integrated with the main spacecraft, which was developed by the UAE Space Agency. Faisal Al Bannai, secretary-general of the Advanced Technology Research Council, and Ahmad Belhoul Al Falasi (left), chairman of the UAE Space Agency, sign a model of the lander that will fly on the Emirates Mission to the Asteroid Belt, which is scheduled to launch in March 2028. (Image credit: TII) If all goes to plan, the mission will lift off from Japan in March 2028, kicking off the Emirates Mission to the Asteroid Belt (EMA). The project is an ambitious follow-up to the UAE Space Agency's Hope Mars orbiter , which has been studying the Red Planet since 2021. "It's a proud moment for us here at the UAE," said Faisal al-Bannai, the secretary general of the Advanced Technology Research Council in Abu Dhabi. 'We don't know what we're going to find' EMA will conduct high-speed flybys of six asteroids before reaching and orbiting 269 Justitia . It will travel a total of about 3 billion miles (5 billion kilometers), which is equivalent to circling Earth roughly 125,000 times, said Najwa Aaraj, the CEO of the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, which designed, built and tested the mission's lander.

candidates.raw_excerpt: Video: 00:01:45 Before Rosalind Franklin can explore Mars, it has to get off its lander. Engineers are rehearsing that first journey on Earth, using a full-size rover model and Mars-like terrain. The test recreates some of the challenges Rosalind Franklin will face on the Red Planet, from reduced gravity and a 20-degree incline to uneven ground and obstacles beneath its ramps. In 2030, Rosalind Franklin will make this journey for real on Mars.
